subject: Biochemistry
question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with megaloblastic anaemia, orotic aciduria, and normal ammonia levels. He was previously healthy. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible?
explanation: UMP synthase deficiency (orotic aciduria type I) impairs the conversion of orotic acid to UMP in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Because the urea cycle is intact, ammonia levels are normal — distinguishing this from urea cycle disorders. OTC and CPS-I deficiencies cause hyperammonaemia. The megaloblastic anaemia results from impaired pyrimidine synthesis required for DNA replication. Treatment: oral uridine supplementation.

subject: Pathology
question_text: A 55-year-old man undergoes surgery for colon cancer. The tumour is found to have microsatellite instability (MSI-H). Which syndrome is most likely responsible if this is a hereditary cancer?
explanation: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes — MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2. Defective MMR leads to microsatellite instability (MSI-H). It is the most common hereditary colon cancer syndrome. FAP is caused by APC mutations and produces hundreds of polyps (microsatellite stable). Peutz-Jeghers involves STK11 mutations with hamartomatous polyps. Cowden involves PTEN mutations.

subject: Pharmacology
question_text: A patient is started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis. Which vitamin supplement should be given concurrently to prevent a common side effect?
explanation: Isoniazid inhibits pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) metabolism, leading to peripheral neuropathy through depletion of pyridoxine. Pyridoxine (B6) 25–50 mg/day is given concurrently to prevent this side effect. Patients at highest risk include malnourished individuals, alcoholics, diabetics, and pregnant women. Isoniazid can also cause hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs) and drug-induced lupus.

subject: Immunology
question_text: A 6-month-old boy has recurrent bacterial and fungal infections since birth. Lab shows absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity is undetectable. Which inheritance pattern explains this condition?
explanation: ADA deficiency causes SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) through autosomal recessive inheritance. ADA deficiency leads to accumulation of deoxyadenosine, which is selectively toxic to lymphocytes (T, B, and NK cells), explaining the complete lymphocyte absence. X-linked SCID (most common form) is caused by γc chain mutations — but ADA deficiency specifically is autosomal recessive. Treatment: gene therapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

subject: Anatomy
question_text: A patient undergoes a posterior hip dislocation after a high-impact motor vehicle accident. Which nerve is most commonly injured in this type of dislocation?
explanation: The sciatic nerve exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, passing posterior to the hip joint. In posterior hip dislocations, the femoral head is displaced posteriorly and superiorly, directly compressing or stretching the sciatic nerve. This results in foot drop (common peroneal division most affected), weakness of knee flexors, and sensory loss over the posterior thigh, leg, and foot. The femoral nerve exits anteriorly and is injured in anterior dislocations.
